Use a restricted mathematical parser and enforce limits before evaluation. Observed validation accepted `2 * (3 + 4)` and rejected `__import__('os').getcwd()`. These two checks demonstrate grammar behavior; they do not establish evaluator security.

For your Python integration:
- Avoid `eval()` and `exec()`. Allow only required numeric literals, operators, variables, and explicitly approved mathematical functions; reject imports, attribute access, and arbitrary calls.
- Call `validate_syntax(expression)` or `evaluate(expression, validate_only=True)`. Reject reported validation errors even when the tool response has `isError: false`. Evaluate the same expression using the same strict grammar only after all checks pass.
- Bound input length, nesting, operation count, exponent size, and numeric magnitude. Apply CPU, memory, and wall-clock limits in an isolated worker; rate-limit requests.
- Handle division by zero, domain errors, overflow, and non-finite results with controlled errors. Avoid exposing tracebacks or recording sensitive expressions in logs.
- Pin and scan dependencies, run with least privilege, and test rejected Python constructs, oversized inputs, expensive expressions, and arithmetic errors.

These controls follow OWASP guidance on injection prevention, input validation, denial-of-service protection, error handling, and dependency management. See the [Input Validation Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html) and [Denial of Service Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Denial_of_Service_Cheat_Sheet.html).

The security tool produced an assessment template, not findings from your codebase. No source code was supplied or audited.
